апельсинные штиблеты.finding: Штиблеты (from German Stiefel) are men's low laced ankle boots or dress shoes, and in 20th-century Russian the word already carried a slightly dated, jocular tone (Wiktionary: 'usually plural, ironic/humorous'; MAS entry unreachable). In ch. V of Двенадцать стульев Bender first appears with 'ноги были в лаковых штиблетах с замшевым верхом апельсинного цвета' and no socks, and the shortened epithet 'апельсинные штиблеты' recurs ('Остап надел на голые ноги апельсинные штиблеты'). Commentators (Arzamas, CyberLeninka) read the orange as a NEP-era fashion marker: light, near-yellow 'джимми/шимми' boots and the 'tango' orange craze of the 1920s, i.e. a poor man's flash. The unusual adjective апельсинный (rather than оранжевый) is part of the deadpan comedy and is the detail a 2013 Russian reader still recognised as Bender's signature. The established English rendering (Richardson, 1961) is 'patent-leather boots with orange-coloured suede uppers'; I could not verify online how the Fisher (2011), Zhang Peiwen (Chinese) or Egawa Takashi (Japanese) editions word it.

rendering.ja: オレンジ色の編み上げ靴

апельсинные штиблеты.note_for_reader: Штиблеты: low laced ankle boots; bright orange-yellow footwear was a NEP-era dandy fashion, so the epithet marks Bender as a flashy man with no socks.
апельсинные штиблеты.rationale: Kept the denotation (ankle boots, not shoes or tall boots: en 'boots' follows Richardson, zh 短靴 and ja 編み上げ靴 avoid 皮靴/短靴 which read as tall boots or plain low shoes) and a single fixed colour epithet to recur book-wide; gave up the odd fruit-adjective 'apelsinnyi' and the dated humorous flavour of штиблеты, which the note supplies.

Категория:Двенадцать стульев (Ильф и Пет.finding: This is not a phrase from the novel. It is the MediaWiki category link that appears in the category box at the foot of every chapter page of the Russian Wikisource (Викитека) edition of Двенадцать стульев; 'Категория:' is the Category namespace prefix, and the category groups the 53 pages of the work (title page, Главы I–XL, the 1928 '30 дней' serial parts and the ЗиФ 1928 parts) under the parents 'Русская проза', 'Проза Ильфа и Петрова' and 'Романы'. Russian Wikisource help describes categories as a navigation tool ('составлять автоматические оглавления'); a Russian reader in 2013 saw it as site chrome, exactly as an English reader sees 'Category: ...' on Wikipedia, carrying no literary meaning. The same footer also carries hidden maintenance categories (PD-old-70, 100%, Страницы без сканов). The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte coverage does not apply to this term. The translators' proposals (omit / 削除) already agree: the string is scraping residue and must be removed from the edition, not rendered.
Категория:Двенадцать стульев (Ильф и Пет.rationale: The string is a Wikisource category footer, not authorial text, so the edition should delete the whole line in all three targets; the bound rendering is empty rather than '(omit)' so that no placeholder leaks into the printed page. Nothing of denotation, connotation or register is lost because none belongs to the novel; if the pipeline requires a visible token, use '(omit)' / '（删除）' / '（削除）' as an internal marker only.

Воробьянинов.finding: Surname of Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov (b. 1875, Stargorod district), the former uyezd marshal of the nobility who in 1927 is a ZAGS registrar in town N and, with Ostap Bender, hunts the twelve chairs; his childhood nickname Kisa is what Bender calls him. The narrator uses the bare surname when he acts, the name-and-patronymic when others address him, and the novel makes him a physical double of the Kadet leader Pavel Milyukov (hence the pince-nez) and Bender's mock 'giant of thought, father of Russian democracy'. For a Russian reader of 2013 the surname was proverbial through the novel and the Gaidai (1971) and Zakharov (1976) films: it stands for a faded gentleman of the old regime, pompous and helpless. English coverage (Wikipedia, Northwestern UP for Fisher's 2011 translation) uniformly spells it Vorobyaninov. Both published Chinese translations checked (张佩文, 人民文学出版社 2004; 徐昌翰, 江苏凤凰文艺 2022) use 沃洛比亚尼诺夫; the proposed 沃罗比扬尼诺夫 is not attested in any edition found. Japanese is split: Egawa Takashi's 1961/1966 translation has ボロビヤニノフ, current film and press coverage has ヴォロビヤニノフ (Morc Asagaya) or ヴォロビャニノフ (RBTH Japan).
Воробьянинов.note_for_reader: Vorobyaninov is the surname of Ippolit Matveyevich; Russian narration alternates surname, name-and-patronymic and the nickname Kisa for the same man.
Воробьянинов.rationale: Denotation is kept by binding one fixed spelling per language and using it wherever the Russian has the bare surname, so it stays visibly the same man as 'Ippolit Matveyevich' and 'Kisa'; the English follows the only spelling in print, the Chinese follows both published translations rather than the unattested proposal, and the Japanese takes the modern ヴォ form used in current coverage over Egawa's older ボ. The sparrow (воробей) echo in the name and its proverbial ring for Russians are given up; nothing in transliteration can carry them.

Виктор Михайлович Полесов.finding: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov is a fictional character of The Twelve Chairs (ch. X, 'Слесарь, попугай и гадалка'), a Stargorod 'слесарь-интеллигент' (mechanic-intellectual) who runs a private workshop 'Слесарная мастерская и починка примусов' and is the clumsiest of the NEP-era 'кустари с мотором' (licensed one-man artisans); he builds a motorcycle out of car, fire-extinguisher, bicycle and typewriter parts that stalls at once, abandons Starkomkhoz orders, and meddles in everything. A monarchist busybody, he assembles the former elite for Bender's fake 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare' and is made 'trustee of the educational district'. For Russian readers the name is a byword for the hyperactive incompetent tinkerer; the narrator alternates the surname with the respectful name-plus-patronymic for mock-solemn effect. Existing English translations (Richardson 1961 on lib.ru: 'V.M. Polesov', chapter 'The Mechanic, the Parrot, and the Fortune-teller'; Fisher 2011) keep the name transliterated; Chinese editions (上海译文) title the chapter '钳工、鹦鹉和女巫'; the Japanese standard is Egawa Takashi's 江川卓 translation 『十二の椅子』. Search did not surface the exact zh/ja spellings of the surname in those editions, so the proposed katakana/hanzi are standard transliterations rather than verified established ones.

Виктор Михайлович Полесов.note_for_reader: Polesov, a self-employed Stargorod mechanic; the narrator's 'Viktor Mikhailovich' (name + patronymic, a polite address) and 'Polesov' are the same man.
Виктор Михайлович Полесов.rationale: Full transliteration in all three languages keeps denotation and the ironic register of the polite name-patronymic form; bind the short forms too (en 'Polesov'/'Viktor Mikhailovich', zh '波列索夫'/'维克托·米哈伊洛维奇', ja 'ポレーソフ'/'ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ') so both narrator forms map to one person, and carry the 'mechanic-intellectual' epithet in the text rather than the name. Given up: no proverbial resonance of the name for target readers.

Заседание продолжается.finding: Ostap Bender's catchphrase, first spoken in ch. VI («Бриллиантовый дым») when the drunk janitor Tikhon starts singing instead of answering: «Придется отложить опрос свидетелей до утра. Заседание продолжается. Будем спать.» He repeats it through the book, often as «Заседание продолжается, господа присяжные заседатели», mock-chairing his own swindle as if it were a committee or a court. Dushenko's dictionary of quotations traces it to the words of Charles Dupuy, president of the French Chamber of Deputies, after the anarchist Vaillant's bomb on 9 December 1893 — «Messieurs, la séance continue!» — a phrase that reached Russia via the press (it was misattributed to Duma chairman Muromtsev in 1906) and that Ilf and Petrov's readers knew as a stock formula of unflappable officialdom. Today it is a Russian proverb meaning 'the important business goes on regardless'. English coverage renders it 'The session continues!' or, in Richardson's 1961 translation, 'The hearing is continued!'; the 2021 Shanghai Translation edition (tr. 白桦熊) uses 庭审继续进行 and other Chinese coverage uses 会议继续进行; no Japanese rendering (Egawa Takashi's 1969 translation) could be located online. The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.
Заседание продолжается.note_for_reader: Ostap's refrain parodies a chairman's formula for resuming after an interruption (famously Dupuy's 'la séance continue' after the 1893 bomb in the French Chamber); it is now a Russian proverb.
Заседание продолжается.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a meeting resumes) and the deadpan official register, which is where the joke lives; 'session'/会议/会議 stay neutral enough to cover both Ostap's committee and courtroom framings, so we reject Richardson's 'hearing' and the 2021 Chinese 庭审, which lock in a court reading. What is given up is the reader's instant recognition of the Dupuy allusion and its proverb status, hence the one-line note; the wording must be identical at every occurrence.

«Нимфа».finding: «Нимфа» is the fictional rival funeral parlour in the county town of N. in chapter I of Двенадцать стульев: its silver coffins gleam behind wavy greenish glass across the street from the dusty oak coffins of the coffin-maker Bezenchuk, and it is owned by three partners who bow in chorus to Vorobyaninov and later trail him hoping for his mother-in-law's funeral. Bezenchuk calls it a 'business of three families living off one little trade' whose brocade is inferior and whose tassels are 'thin', while his own firm dates from 1907. The joke for a 1928 reader is the NEP-era private undertaker's pretentious classical shop-sign, a Greek nature-goddess of youth and beauty on a coffin shop, which the narrators deadpan and the chapter title turns into a mock-plural, 'Безенчук и «нимфы»', naming the three owners after their sign. The established renderings are consistent: John Richardson's English (1961) has 'the Nymph Funeral Home' and 'the three Nymphs'; the Northwestern (Fisher, 2011) edition also titles the chapter 'Bezenchuk and the Nymphs'; Chinese editions vary between '山林女神' (徐昌翰, 江苏凤凰文艺 2022) and '仙女' (上海译文 2022); the Japanese rendering in the Egawa Takashi translation (筑摩書房 1969 / 集英社 1966) could not be verified online, but katakana ニンフ is the ordinary Japanese word for nymph.
«Нимфа».note_for_reader: A nymph is a Greek goddess of springs and woods, youth and beauty: a grotesquely cheerful name for a coffin shop, typical of NEP-era private trade.
«Нимфа».rationale: All three keep the denotation (a shop named after the Greek nymph) and the mock-classical register, so the chapter-title pun 'Bezenchuk and the Nymphs' / «宁芙们» / ニンフたち still works; Chinese loses the immediate transparency that 仙女 or 山林女神 would give, which the one-line note restores, and the added 殡葬社/葬儀社 supplies the 'funeral parlour' the Russian reader inferred from context.

Великий комбинатор.finding: Bender's book-long epithet, first used as the title of Chapter V and repeated in mock-solemn narration ('Великий комбинатор танцевал танго'). 'Комбинатор' (from 'комбинация' = a shady deal, a scheme) was in the 1900s–1920s marked as Odessa/Jewish commercial slang and carried a 'colloquial' label in Russian dictionaries; by 1928 it had gone general, and 'великий' gives it the mock-grandeur of 'Великий инквизитор' or 'Пётр Великий'. After the novels the phrase became a proverbial Russian tag for any resourceful con man or over-clever schemer. Existing renderings: both complete English translations of The Twelve Chairs (John Richardson 1961; Anne O. Fisher 2011, Northwestern) use 'the smooth operator', with Chapter V titled 'The Smooth Operator'; the 2009 Open Letter Golden Calf uses 'the grand strategist'; Wikipedia and scholarship gloss it literally as 'the Great Combinator'. Chinese: 张佩文 (人民文学 2004) titles Ch. 5 '伟大谋士', 白桦熊 (上海译文 2022) '了不起的幕僚'; no fixed Chinese phrase. Japanese: 江川卓's translation (筑摩 1961/1969) is the only one; reference works call Bender 大詐欺師 and readers describe him as 策士, but no single fixed Japanese epithet is established.
Великий комбинатор.note_for_reader: Russian velikiy kombinator, literally 'the great combinator', a maker of shady 'combinations' (schemes); after these novels the phrase became proverbial for any resourceful con man.
Великий комбинатор.rationale: English binds the rendering used by every published English Twelve Chairs, so the epithet is recognisable and works as a chapter title and a repeated tag, at the cost of the literal 'combinations' and some of the mock-imperial 'great' (restored by the note). Chinese and Japanese keep the mock-solemn 'great' and the scheming denotation (谋略/策) in a form that reads naturally as a title and matches the tone of the existing Chinese chapter titles; they give up the Odessa-slang colouring and the con-man bluntness of 骗子/詐欺師, which the narration itself supplies.

Старкомхоз.finding: Старкомхоз is a fictional Soviet-style stump compound: Стар(городский) + ком(мунальное) + хоз(яйство), i.e. the Stargorod Department of Communal Economy, the municipal-services office under the town soviet that ran trams, housing, water, cleaning and the like. Комхоз/горкомхоз/губкоммунхоз were real 1920s administrative abbreviations (Mokienko & Nikitina, Толковый словарь языка Совдепии, cite Mayakovsky's 'канцупрдел Комхоза'), and Ilf and Petrov coin the Stargorod version alongside Старсобес and Мельстрой. It appears in Chapter XIII ('Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!'): Treukhov takes his tram project 'к новому заведующему Старкомхозом Гаврилину, которого перевели в Старгород из Самарканда', and 'Грузовики Старкомхоза и Мельстроя развозили детей'. For a Russian reader the humour is in the clunky acronym itself and in Gavrilin, the provincial boss who thinks a donkey beats a tram. The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte coverage does not apply to this term; no such coverage exists. The public-domain English (Richardson) renders it descriptively as 'the Stargorod communal services', dropping the acronym; Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation could not be checked online; no published Chinese or Japanese rendering was found.

rendering.zh: 斯塔尔科姆霍兹（斯塔尔戈罗德市公用事业局）
rendering.ja: スタルコムホーズ（スタルゴロド市公共事業局）

Старкомхоз.note_for_reader: Starkomkhoz: a mock Soviet acronym, STARgorod KOMmunal KHOZyaistvo, the town's municipal-services department; expansion given at first mention, the bare acronym reused thereafter.
Старкомхоз.rationale: Keeps the denotation (municipal services department) via the parenthetical expansion at first use and keeps the officialese connotation and the running gag of Star- acronyms (Starsobes, Starkomkhoz) by retaining the transliterated stump compound as the book-wide short form; gives up the instant transparency Richardson gets from 'communal services', and 'Municipal/公用事业/公共事業' loses the specifically Soviet word 'communal', which would mislead English readers.

Клавдия Ивановна.finding: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova is Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law (тёща), the elderly widow who dies in chapter 2 in the town of N and, on her deathbed, tells both her son-in-law and Father Fyodor that she sewed the family jewels into one of the twelve Gambs dining chairs during the Revolution; her death sets the whole plot in motion. The text alternates between the respectful name-and-patronymic form (how the narrator and Vorobyaninov address her) and the bare kinship word тёща, and the comic contrast between the two registers (a dead mother-in-law is a stock Russian joke) is part of the humour, so the reader must be able to link them. Existing English translations do not agree: John Richardson (1961, the freely circulated text) writes 'Claudia Ivanovna', while Wikipedia/Wikidata and secondary coverage use 'Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova'; I could not open the Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) text to check her spelling. Chinese editions mostly refer to her by surname as 佩图霍娃太太 (Shanghai Translation 2022 chapter title 佩图霍娃太太辞世; Houlang/Xu Changhan edition) or 别图霍娃 (Zhang Peiwen, People's Literature 2004 blurb); no Chinese or Japanese page I could reach shows the given-name-plus-patronymic form, and the Egawa Takashi Japanese translation (Chikuma 1969) is not online, so the ja/zh renderings below are standard transliterations rather than attested ones.

rendering.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
rendering.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ

Клавдия Ивановна.note_for_reader: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova: Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law (Russian тёща), the original owner of the twelve chairs; name-and-patronymic is the polite way to address an older person.
Клавдия Ивановна.rationale: Keeps denotation and the formal name-and-patronymic register by transliterating rather than Latinising to 'Claudia' (which hides the Russian in a side-by-side edition and breaks the link to the zh/ja forms); the mother-in-law connotation cannot live in the name itself, so it is carried by rendering тёща consistently as mother-in-law / 岳母 / 義母 and by the one-line note at first occurrence.

Большая Пушкинская.finding: Bolshaya Pushkinskaya is the pre-revolutionary name of a main street in the fictional Stargorod (a composite of Starobelsk and Odessa). It appears in ch. V as a Soviet renaming joke: Ostap 'вышел на Красноармейскую (бывшая Большая Пушкинская)', in a passage that also lists улица Ленских событий (бывшая Денисовская), Кооперативная and two separate Советская streets; in ch. XIII the narrator quietly reverts to the old name when the new tram 'свернули на Большую Пушкинскую'. For a 1928 reader the point was the wave of ideological street renamings of the 1920s, and that townspeople (and the narrators) kept using the old names; 'Большая' is a standard old-Russian street prefix (as in Bolshaya Morskaya), not an evaluative adjective. John Richardson's standard English translation translates the whole set: 'He passed along Soviet Street, came out into Red Army Street (previously Greater Pushkin Street)', 'Co-operative Street', 'Lena Massacre Street'. I could not verify Anne O. Fisher's (2011) wording for this street online, nor a published Chinese or Japanese rendering of it; the zh/ja proposals below follow ordinary conventions (大…街 / 大…通り).
Большая Пушкинская.note_for_reader: Stargorod's streets were renamed in the 1920s (Red Army Street, Soviet Street, Lena Massacre Street); the narrators and townspeople keep slipping back to the old names.
Большая Пушкинская.rationale: Book-wide rule: translate every Stargorod street name (old and new) and the word 'street', because the joke lives in the meaning of the Soviet names ('Red Army', 'Lena Massacre', two 'Soviet' streets) and a transliterated 'Krasnoarmeyskaya' would kill it for a non-Russianist; this keeps denotation and the ironic connotation and matches the proposed zh/ja forms, which already translate 'Bolshaya' as 大. Given up: the Russian sound of the name and the transliteration convention used for real streets (Bolshaya Morskaya), acceptable because Stargorod is fictional; 'Great' is preferred to Richardson's 'Greater', which falsely implies a paired 'Lesser Pushkin Street'.

2-й дом Старсобеса.finding: Старсобес = Старгородский (отдел) социального обеспечения: 'собес' is a 1920–23 Soviet abbreviation for the local social-welfare office (Wiktionary marks it colloquial, a Sovietism, associated with pensioners and bureaucracy), and Стар- is the fictional town Stargorod. The '2nd Home' is a state almshouse for about fifteen old women, housed in Vorobyaninov's former mansion, run by the blushing thief Alkhen; its real prototype was an almshouse on Armyansky Lane in Moscow described to Ilf by a Gudok colleague. For a Russian reader the portmanteau itself is the joke: a stately private house reduced to a numbered line in a welfare ledger, and 'собес' still reads as shabby-officialese today. Both published English translations expand it: Richardson (1961) 'Second Social Security Home' (sign: 'SECOND SOCIAL SECURITY HOME OF THE STAR-PROV-INS-AD'), Fisher (2011) 'the Second Stargorod Social Security Home'. Searches found no quotable Chinese (Zhang Peiwen 2004) or Japanese (Egawa Takashi 1969) wording for the term, so the zh/ja renderings are built by analogy, not attested.

rendering.en: the Second Stargorod Social Security Home
rendering.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社保第二养老院
rendering.ja: スタルゴロド社会保障第二養老院

2-й дом Старсобеса.note_for_reader: Starsobes: 'Stargorod Social Welfare Office', a typical 1920s Soviet portmanteau; the 'Home' is a state almshouse for old women.
2-й дом Старсобеса.rationale: Keeps denotation (Stargorod + welfare office + numbered almshouse) and the deadpan bureaucratic register by using an established English formula and compact kanji/hanzi compounds (社保/社会保障 mimic the Soviet abbreviation); gives up the portmanteau's sound and the bare 'Starsobes' transliteration, which carries nothing for the target reader.

Муза дальних странствий.finding: The phrase is a quotation from Nikolai Gumilyov's poem 'Отъезжающему' (1913, first in the journal Giperborei, then in the collection 'Колчан'): 'Ведь ты во всём её убранстве / Увидел Музу Дальних Странствий' — a capitalised, lyrical personification of the pull of far-off voyages, typical of Gumilyov's Acmeist exoticism. Ilf and Petrov made it a chapter title (Part I, ch. 4) and re-use it in the text with deadpan solemnity: 'Муза дальних странствий манит человека. Уже вырвала она отца Федора из тихой уездной обители и бросила невесть в какую губернию.' The joke is the gap between the Silver Age muse and the shabby NEP-era rail journeys of a defrocking priest and an ex-marshal; commentators tie it to the novel's recurring explorer motif (the 'Columbus' theater, 'Traces of the Titanic'). Serov's dictionary of winged words records that the expression became proverbial in Russian precisely through Ilf and Petrov, as a semi-ironic label for wanderlust; by the 2010s a Russian reader knew it as a stock phrase, and many would not recall Gumilyov (a poet shot in 1921 and unpublished in the USSR for decades). Existing translations: Richardson (1961) 'The Muse of Travel', Fisher (2011) 'The Muse of Distant Travel'; the current Chinese edition (Shanghai Translation, 2021) titles the chapter '远游的缪斯'. No Japanese chapter title (Egawa Taku's 1969 translation) could be verified online.
Муза дальних странствий.note_for_reader: A line from Gumilyov's 1913 poem 'To One Departing'; the novel turns the poet's grand muse of far voyages into a running deadpan joke about third-class rail travel.
Муза дальних странствий.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a personified muse of far journeys) and the mock-elevated register, with the capitalised 'Muse'/缪斯/ミューズ so every later mention echoes the chapter title; the English 'Distant Wanderings' is preferred over Fisher's flatter 'Distant Travel' because 'странствия' is wanderings and the lyric pitch is the joke, the Chinese follows the established 2021 edition, and the Japanese uses archaic 遠き to supply the poetic tone. What is given up is the reader's recognition of Gumilyov as source, which no rendering can carry and which the note supplies.

Старгико.finding: Старгико is a fictional Stargorod shop name appearing three times: ch. IX (a Red Army platoon crosses 'a puddle beginning at the Stargiko store'), ch. X (the fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna, not the widow, complains 'Now there are only queues, no shops, and the names of these shops are the most dreadful. Stargiko!..'), and ch. XXVII (Alkhen 'pumps' half a pood of sugar out of the Stargiko store and moves his queue 'to another co-operative'). It is a parody of the 1920s mania for syllabic acronyms (cf. the real Старгубстрах / 'Стар-губ-страх-касса' sign nearby): the Odessky–Feldman commentary conjectures Stargorod + ГИКО, a provincial co-operative association of invalids (губернское кооперативное объединение инвалидов), which ran its own shops in the 1920s. For a 1928 reader it connoted NEP-era co-operative retail, rationing queues and shortages, and the ugliness of Soviet bureaucratic naming; nothing beyond that is settled. Richardson's standard English translation (1961/1965) keeps 'Stargiko!' in ch. X and paraphrases 'the Stargorod co-operative shop' in ch. IX. I found no online text of the Fisher (2011), 张佩文 (Chinese) or 江川卓 (Japanese) versions to check their forms.

rendering.zh: 斯塔尔吉科（斯塔尔戈罗德合作社）
rendering.ja: スタルギコ（スタルゴロド協同組合）

Старгико.note_for_reader: Stargiko: a typical 1920s Soviet syllabic acronym for a Stargorod co-operative store; the joke is that such names were ugly and opaque even to locals.
Старгико.rationale: Kept denotation (a co-op shop) and register (an ugly, opaque bureaucratic acronym, transliterated so it stays alien in all three scripts, with the one-word 'Co-op' expansion at first use only); gave up the conjectural 'invalids' association' detail, which the commentary itself marks as probable and which no established translation carries.

Тихон.finding: Tikhon is the old дворник (yard-keeper/caretaker) of Vorobyaninov's former house in Stargorod, met in chapter V ('Великий комбинатор'): when Vorobyaninov turns up he bellows 'Барин! Из Парижа!', reminisces about the three-rouble tips at New Year and Easter and the medal his master promised him, and is then got drunk and bribed with a paper rouble by Bender, who learns from him that the chairs went to the housing department and one chair to the almshouse. His speech is servile, uneducated and pre-revolutionary ('барин', filler 'буду говорить'), which in 1928 marks him as a comic relic of the old order still loyal to a vanished master. The name itself was common among the lower classes in pre-revolutionary Russia (Greek 'fortunate'), and to a 1920s reader also echoed Patriarch Tikhon, whose loyalists Soviet propaganda called 'тихоновщина' — a faint churchy, old-regime flavour that fits the character but is not a pun the text exploits. The character is well established in English coverage as 'Tikhon' (IMDb credits Yuri Nikulin as 'Tikhon, street cleaner' in the 1971 film); Japanese standard transliteration is チーホン (as for 総主教チーホン); Chinese uses 吉洪 (as for 吉洪牧首), though I could not open a Chinese edition page to confirm the novel's translators' choice.
Тихон.note_for_reader: Tikhon, the old yard-keeper, still calls Vorobyaninov 'barin' (master), the pre-revolutionary address of servants to gentry, a decade after such masters were abolished.
Тихон.rationale: The name is transliterated by the established conventions in all three languages, keeping denotation and consistency; the servile, old-regime register cannot live in the name and must be carried by his speech (rendering 'барин' as 'master'/'老爷'/'旦那様' rather than transliterating it), while the faint echo of Patriarch Tikhon is given up as untranslatable and not load-bearing.

Брильянтовый дым.finding: Title of Part I, Chapter VI of Двенадцать стульев (Chapter 7 in editions that restore the cut opening chapter). Not an idiom or period slang: it is the authors' own mock-lyrical image, picked up by the chapter's opening lines ('Брильянтовый дым держался под потолком. Жемчужные бусы катились по столу... Драгоценный мираж потрясал комнату') for the hallucinatory greed that fills Tikhon's filthy porter's lodge as Vorobyaninov inventories his mother-in-law's jewels and Ostap haggles his cut up to 40 percent. Брильянтовый with one л is a pre-reform/1920s variant spelling (Ushakov marks it; modern norm is бриллиантовый), so it reads as period colour to a Russian reader, not as an error. Established renderings: John Richardson's 1961 English has 'A Diamond Haze'; Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern edition has 'Diamond Smoke'; Chinese editions diverge (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022: 钻石迷雾; 徐昌翰, 江苏凤凰文艺 2022: 钻石的清辉; 张佩文, 人民文学 2004 is reported as 钻石迷雾 but I could not verify the page). No Japanese chapter title could be verified online; the Egawa Taku (江川卓) 1969 Chikuma translation exists but its table of contents is not indexed.
Брильянтовый дым.rationale: Kept the denotation and the deliberately overwrought, mock-poetic image (smoke/mist of diamonds) and aligned en with Fisher's current standard translation and zh with the 2022 上海译文 edition; gave up the old-spelling period colour of брильянтовый, which no target language can mark without a note the image does not need.

Старопанская площадь.finding: Fictional central square of Stargorod in The Twelve Chairs: chapter I has the crowd gossiping about Klavdia Ivanovna's stroke 'посреди Старопанской площади, у бюстика поэта Жуковского', and chapter II has the fire brigade emerging from it and the smoking Gos. No. 1 car standing at its corner with 'улица имени товарища Губернского'. The name is a plausible old-regime toponym: 'Старые Паны' was the Polish (pan) quarter of Moscow's Kitai-gorod, whence the real Старопанский переулок (renamed so in 1922), so to a Russian reader the square sounds pre-revolutionary and unrenamed, in deliberate contrast with the freshly Sovietised 'Comrade Gubernsky Street'; the etymology is background colour, not a joke that needs carrying. Commentators disagree on Stargorod's prototype (one LiveJournal essay maps the square onto Kyiv's Tsarskaya Square); nothing canonical. English precedent is split: John Richardson (1961) uses 'Staropan Square', while the passage as quoted from Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation reads 'Staropanskaya Square'. I found no online text of the Chinese (上海译文) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) versions showing their rendering.

rendering.ja: スタロパンスカヤ広場

Старопанская площадь.rationale: Keeps denotation (a fixed, recognisable proper name that recurs identically across chapters) and the neutral toponymic register by full transliteration, matching the most recent scholarly English translation and standard zh/ja transcription conventions; gives up the faint 'Old Polish quarter' connotation, which a Russian reader of 2013 barely registers either, so no note is warranted.

«Сорбонна».finding: In the novel «Сорбонна» is the name of the Stargorod lodging house where Bender and Vorobyaninov (and, separately, Father Fyodor) stay: the text introduces it as «меблированные комнаты „Сорбонна"» (furnished rooms, ch. XI), Ostap inspects 7-, 5- and 3-rouble rooms and settles for one at 1 r. 80 k. with two beds and a night-table, and later chapters call it a гостиница and номера; a wagon carries its name and out-of-town delegates lodge there for the tram opening. The joke is purely onomastic: a provincial flophouse with shabby carpets and a bad smell wearing the name of the Paris university, the kind of pretentious pre-revolutionary trade name (like 'Hotel Bristol' or 'Europe') that survived into NEP. No commentary found online (Shcheglov's and Odessky/Feldman's annotations are not freely available) points to a real prototype; the Starobelsk-as-Stargorod article names no hotel. Richardson's 1961 English translation renders it as 'the Sorbonne Furnished Rooms' at first mention and thereafter 'the Sorbonne Hotel' / 'the Sorbonne', and Fisher's 2011 translation also uses 'the Sorbonne Hotel'. I could not retrieve the text of the Chinese (张佩文, 人民文学出版社 2004) or Japanese (江川卓, 筑摩書房) translations, so no established zh/ja rendering of the hotel name is confirmed; the proposed renderings use the standard transliterations of the university (索邦, ソルボンヌ). The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte and 2013 does not apply to this term.
«Сорбонна».note_for_reader: A cheap provincial lodging house grandly named after the Paris university.
«Сорбонна».rationale: All three keep the denotation (recognisably 'Sorbonne', in quotation marks as a proper name) and the ironic mismatch of grand name on shabby premises, which needs no gloss for a reader who knows the Sorbonne; English follows Richardson/Fisher ('the Sorbonne', expanded to 'the Sorbonne Hotel' or 'furnished rooms' only where the Russian itself says гостиница/меблированные комнаты). Given up: the specific NEP flavour of меблированные комнаты/номера as a class of lodging, which zh 旅馆 and ja ホテル flatten to a generic hotel; a one-line note covers the first mention.

Ипполит Матвеевич / Воробьянинов.finding: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov is the novel's co-protagonist: born 1875, a former uyezdny predvoditel dvoryanstva (district marshal of the nobility) of Stargorod, reduced after 1917 to a registrar of deaths and marriages at the ZAGS office of the town of N, living with his mother-in-law; 52 years old, tall, grey, moustached, resembling the Kadet politician Milyukov. Ostap seizes on his childhood nickname Kisa and also calls him 'field marshal' and 'district marshal of the Comanches'; the narrator's mock-solemn alternation of name-patronymic and surname is itself the joke, since the full ceremonial form is applied to a helpless ex-gentleman. By 2013 'Kisa Vorobyaninov' was a household name in Russia via Gaidai's 1971 film (Sergei Filippov) and Zakharov's 1976 film (Anatoly Papanov), a byword for a faded, greedy, helpless former gentleman. English is settled: Richardson (1961) and Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) both print 'Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov', as does English Wikipedia. Chinese editions split: Zhang Peiwen (People's Literature, 2004) and Xu Changhan (2022) use 沃洛比亚尼诺夫 (Xu shortens the given name to 伊坡利), and Baidu Baike/Douban follow that, while at least one other edition prints 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫. Japanese coverage (Egawa Takashi's translation, Gaidai film screenings, reader blogs) consistently uses ヴォロビヤニノフ and オスタップ・ベンデル; an older review renders the given name イポリット・マトベイッチ.

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 / 沃洛比亚尼诺夫
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ / ヴォロビヤニノフ

Ипполит Матвеевич / Воробьянинов.note_for_reader: Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility (elected head of a district's gentry before 1917); Ostap's nickname for him, Kisa, is a childhood pet name meaning 'kitty'.
Ипполит Матвеевич / Воробьянинов.rationale: Denotation and the ceremonial name-patronymic/surname alternation are kept exactly, using the spellings already fixed by Richardson/Fisher in English, by the People's Literature and 2022 Chinese editions (沃洛, not the 新华社-style 沃罗), and by Japanese film and book coverage; the pre-revolutionary rank and the Kisa joke cannot live inside the name and are pushed into the note.

батюшка.finding: Батюшка is the everyday, unofficial way Russian Orthodox laypeople address a parish priest (never a deacon or bishop): warm and familiar, used by parishioners who know the priest, as against the neutral 'отец N' and the ceremonial 'Ваше Преподобие'. In Chapter XII of Двенадцать стульев it is Vorobyaninov who says 'Здравствуйте, батюшка' with 'inexpressible sweetness' to his rival Father Fyodor in the hotel corridor, and Fyodor answers with all the sarcasm God gave him: 'Доброе утро, Ипполит Матвеевич'. The joke is that a folksy, affectionate churchgoer's word is used by an ex-marshal of the nobility as a weapon; 'little father' (the dictionary calque) is not what a Russian hears, since the word is unmarked as a diminutive in this use. The standard English translation (Richardson, 1961) renders it simply 'Good morning, Father'; Japanese coverage calls the character フョードル神父 and Chinese coverage 费奥多尔神父, and 神父 is the ordinary word for an Orthodox priest in both languages, so the priestly address is well established in all three targets.
батюшка.rationale: All three keep the denotation (address to an Orthodox priest) and let the surrounding 'inexpressible sweetness' carry the irony; English 'Father' follows the established Richardson rendering and the Japanese さん recovers some of the familiar warmth, while Chinese 神父 gives up the folksy intimacy entirely because no colloquial Chinese address for a priest exists that would not sound Catholic or invented.

Евпл.finding: Евпл is the monastic name taken by Count Alexei Bulanov, the brilliant Petersburg hussar of Ostap's inserted parable ('Рассказ о гусаре-схимнике'): 'В обители граф Алексей Буланов, принявший имя Евпла, изнурял себя великими подвигами… Подвиг схимника Евпла наполнил удивлением обитель.' The name is that of St Euplius/Euplus of Catania (Greek Εὖπλος, 'good sailing'), a Sicilian archdeacon martyred in 304, commemorated 11 August in the Orthodox calendar; it exists in Russian only as a church-calendar name and was never a living given name, so to a 1928 (or 2013) reader it sounds like an absurdly obscure, clumsy, mock-hagiographic monastic name, part of the parody of saints' lives. The character's chief prototype, the hussar-turned-monk Alexander Bulatovich, actually took the name Antony; Evpl is the authors' comic invention. The parable chapter was cut from Soviet editions after 1928, so the standard Richardson English translation (lib.ru text) contains only the later aside 'Count Alexei Bulanov, the famous hermit hussar' and never renders the name; no established English, Chinese or Japanese rendering could be found in search (Fisher's 2011 full translation was not accessible for checking).
Евпл.note_for_reader: Evpl: monastic name after St Euplus, an obscure 4th-century Sicilian martyr; a real calendar name no Russian ever bore, chosen for its comic clumsiness.
Евпл.rationale: Plain transliteration (Evpl / 叶夫普尔 / エフプル, following standard Russian-to-Chinese and Russian-to-Japanese syllable tables) preserves the deliberately awkward, consonant-clogged sound and the mock-solemn register, and fixes one spelling across the book (Evpl, not Yevpl, as the initial vowel is short and the cluster is the joke); the denotation (the saint Euplus) is given up in the text and recovered in the one-line note, since 'Euplus' would normalise the name into Latin churchiness and lose the Russian oddity.

Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.finding: Fictional co-protagonist of The Twelve Chairs (1928): born 1875, before 1917 a district marshal of the nobility (уездный предводитель дворянства) and stamp collector in the town of Stargorod; after the revolution a registrar of deaths and marriages at the ZAGS office of the town of N, living off his mother-in-law Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova. The narrator names him by name-and-patronymic ('Ипполит Матвеевич') throughout, a mock-respectful formality that Ostap Bender undercuts with the childhood pet-name 'Киса' ('Kitty'); his pince-nez and appearance parody the Kadet politician Milyukov. For a Russian reader of 2013 he is a proverbial figure — the dignified but useless ex-gentleman, the 'гигант мысли, отец русской демократии' of Bender's con — familiar from the novel and the 1971 Gaidai and 1976 Zakharov films. Established renderings: English 'Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov' (Wikipedia, Wikidata, Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation); Chinese editions (张佩文, 人民文学出版社; 白桦熊, 上海译文 2022) write 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 and the surname 沃洛比亚尼诺夫; Japanese: Egawa Takashi's 1966/1969/1977 translation used the old spellings ボロビヤニノフ / イポリット・マトベイッチ, while current Japanese web coverage writes ヴォロビヤニノフ.

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃洛比亚尼诺夫
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.note_for_reader: The narrator's 'Ippolit Matveyevich' (first name + patronymic) is the polite Russian address for a grown man; Bender's 'Kisa' ('Kitty') is his nursery nickname.
Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.rationale: Kept denotation and the mock-formal register by transliterating the full name-and-patronymic in all three languages and matching the spellings already established (English Wikipedia/Fisher; the Chinese surname form 沃洛比亚尼诺夫 used by both published Chinese translations; the surname ヴォロビヤニノフ now standard in Japanese, with modern マトヴェーエヴィチ rather than Egawa's dated マトベイッチ). Given up: the 'sparrow' echo (воробей) in the surname and the automatic comic contrast with 'Kisa', which the reader gets only via the note.

Маховик.finding: In chapter XIII (the Stargorod tramway) the local feuilletonist of the Stargorodskaya Pravda, previously known to the whole town as «Принц Датский» (Prince of Denmark, i.e. Hamlet — a pretentious literary pen-name of the old style), now writes under the new pen-name «Маховик», the Russian word for a flywheel, and the narrators fuse the two as «Принц-Маховик» and «Маховик-Датский». The joke is that a provincial hack has swapped a bookish pseudonym for a fashionable industrial one to suit the era of construction (real 1920s parallel: Olesha signed his Gudok verse «Зубило», Chisel), while his 'production sketches' remain clichéd and technically illiterate — Treukhov's rebuttal mocks 'comrade Makhovik' for thinking rafters hum. The word is transparent to any Russian reader as a machine part, not a surname, so it must be translated, not transliterated. Richardson's standard English translation (1961) renders it 'Flywheel' and 'the Prince of Denmark', with 'The Prince of Denmark (Flywheel)' for the hyphenated form. I could not access the Chinese (张佩文, 人民文学 2004) or Japanese (江川卓, 筑摩 1969) translations' renderings; 飞轮 and はずみ車 are the ordinary dictionary equivalents.
Маховик.note_for_reader: A pen-name (Russian «Маховик», 'flywheel'): the town hack has traded his old literary pseudonym 'Prince of Denmark' (Hamlet) for a suitably industrial one.
Маховик.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a machine part used as a pen-name) and the mock-industrial connotation, matching Richardson's established 'Flywheel' and allowing 'Prince Flywheel' / 飞轮亲王 / はずみ車王子; given up is the sound of a real Russian pseudonym, and in zh/ja the word-play needs the one-line note to land, since 飞轮/はずみ車 do not read as plausible pen-names on their own.

Альхен.finding: Альхен is the pet name by which Александра Яковлевна calls her husband Александр Яковлевич, завхоз of the 2nd Stargorod Social Security Home (an old women's home in the former Vorobyaninov mansion); he calls her Сашхен. Ilf and Petrov introduce him in the chapter titled 'Голубой воришка' as 'застенчивый ворюга': his whole being protests against stealing, yet he cannot not steal, so he steals constantly and blushes constantly (stools, food, brass-band instruments, the home's property). The -хен ending is a mock-German diminutive (as in Gretchen), which to a 1928 Russian reader marked the couple as sentimental petty-bourgeois; 'голубой воришка' became a proverbial phrase for a blushing embezzler. Existing English translations split: John Richardson (1961) writes 'Alchen' / 'Sashchen'; Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) writes 'Alkhen'. Web search did not surface the Chinese (费明君 1954, 张佩文, 徐昌翰, 白桦熊 2021) or Japanese (江川卓 1969/1977) renderings of the nickname, so the zh/ja forms below are phonetic transliterations, not verified against those editions.
Альхен.rationale: Kept as a name in all three languages, matching the current scholarly English (Fisher) and pairing with Sashkhen/萨什亨/サシヘン so the mock-German -khen echo survives; the denotation (Alexander) and the ironic domestic register are carried by the introducing chapter, while the diminutive's petty-bourgeois connotation is given up rather than glossed.

Быстроупак.finding: «Быстроупак» is a fictional NEP-era private packing firm in Stargorod (упаковочная контора), owned by Dyadyev, a former city-duma member; in ch. X its black sign with gold letters hangs on the same house as Kislyarsky's bagel artel, and both, 'despite different signs', actually speculate in textiles (мануфактура). Its 'молодцы' later help arrest the doorman and join the Sword-and-Ploughshare crowd to corner flour and sugar (ch. XXVII), so the name stands for nepman commerce hiding behind a Soviet-sounding contraction of быстрая упаковка. The Odessky–Feldman commentary notes it likely alluded to a real Moscow cooperative artel on Tsvetnoy Boulevard with a near-identical name, «Быструпак», so a 1928 reader heard a real firm-name parody, not a pure invention. Both major English translations translate rather than transliterate: Richardson (1961) 'Fastpack', Fisher (2011) 'Quickpack'. I found no online text of the Chinese (上海译文/张佩文) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) versions to confirm their renderings.
Быстроупак.note_for_reader: Быстроупак = 'quick-packing', a Soviet-style contraction used as a private firm's name; the joke is a nepman shop dressed in official-sounding syllables.
Быстроупак.rationale: All three keep denotation (packing) and the acronym-like compression that carries the mock-Soviet connotation (one closed word: Quickpack; two-character 缩略 快包; 速梱社 in the manner of Japanese abbreviated firm names), and follow the established English choice (Fisher's Quickpack; Richardson's Fastpack is the alternative); given up is the Russian phonetic shape, which the side-by-side Russian line supplies anyway, so the proposed doubled forms Bystroupak (Quick-Pack) / ブィストロウパク（速包社） are dropped as redundant.

Варфоломей Коробейников.finding: A minor character in chapter XI: 'заведующий архивом Варфоломей Коробейников, бывший чиновник канцелярии градоначальства, ныне работник конторского труда' — a former Tsarist town-hall clerk who kept the Stargorod communal-housing (Стакомхоз) furniture requisition orders and now sells them, first to Bender and then to Father Fyodor. He lives in Gusishche, the railwaymen's edge of town, where 'Коробейникова на Гусище звали Варфоломеичем. Обращались к нему только в случае крайней нужды. Варфоломеич брал в залог вещи и назначал людоедские проценты' — a neighbourhood pawnbroker-usurer, one of the novel's gallery of petty schemers (with Alkhen and Kislyarsky); an early draft had him insuring his hundred-year-old grandmother's life and losing on the premiums. The narration itself switches among 'архивариус', 'старик', 'Коробейников' and 'Варфоломеич'; the patronymic-only form is the way a village or working-class street names a known old man, half familiar, half sneering, and here it frames the usurer scenes. English coverage is split: Richardson (1961) anglicises to 'Bartholomew Korobeinikov' / 'Bartholomeich'; the 1971 Gaidai film cast lists (Wikipedia/IMDb) use 'Varfolomey Korobeynikov'; Fisher (2011) transliterates. No Chinese or Japanese rendering of the archivist's name is findable online (the zh/ja Wikipedia and film pages list only actors or protagonists), so zh/ja are built from standard transliteration tables, with コロベイニコフ attested for the surname (pianist Andrei Korobeinikov).

rendering.zh: 瓦尔福洛梅·科罗贝尼科夫／科罗贝尼科夫／瓦尔福洛梅伊奇
rendering.ja: ヴァルフォロメイ・コロベイニコフ／コロベイニコフ／ヴァルフォロメイチ

Варфоломей Коробейников.note_for_reader: Varfolomeich is the patronymic alone (Bartholomew's son) — how a Russian street addresses a familiar old man, here with an edge of contempt for the neighbourhood pawnbroker.
Варфоломей Коробейников.rationale: Kept denotation and the three-form system (full name on introduction, surname in narration, patronymic-only in the Gusishche passages) with a straight transliteration in all three languages, so the side-by-side reader can match the Russian; gave up Richardson's 'Bartholomew/Bartholomeich', which carries the saint's-name flavour but breaks the sound link to the Cyrillic, and gave up the automatic familiar-contempt connotation of a bare patronymic, which no target language has and which the one-line note supplies.

барин.finding: Барин is the pre-revolutionary word for a landowning nobleman, and in a servant's mouth simply 'the master' of the house (Ushakov, sense 1 'помещик, дворянин-землевладелец', marked дореволюц.; sense 4 notes its use as a direct address). By 1927 it survived only as a class slur ('now derogatory' in Ushakov, sense 2) or as a fossil, which is the joke when the drunken yard-keeper Tikhon bellows 'Барин! Из Парижа!' at Vorobyaninov and the narrator then keeps calling him 'барин' through Tikhon's eyes ('Увидя барина в зеленых усах, он перекрестился', ch. VII). Both published English translations render it 'master' (Richardson 1961: '"Master!" bellowed Tikhon with delight. "Back from Paris!"'; Fisher 2011: 'his master first with a black mustache, then with a green one'). Chinese translations of Russian servants' речь conventionally use 老爷 (the servant's address for the male head of household), and it is the reading the 2004 张佩文 and 2022 白桦熊 translations' readers would expect; I could not access the Japanese Egawa Taku translation (筑摩書房 1969) to check its choice, so the ja decision is by convention rather than by citation.
барин.note_for_reader: Barin: the old serf-era word for the lord of the manor; ten years after the Revolution only a servant who never got the news would still say it.
барин.rationale: All three keep the denotation (servant's word for the gentleman of the house) and the old-regime register (master, not 'boss' or 'sir'; 老爷 and 旦那様 are the servant's words of the pre-modern household, whereas 御主人様 reads as modern butler-speak); what is lost is the Soviet-era sting of барин as a class label, which the note restores. 'My master' is dropped in favour of bare 'master' because the vocative 'Master! Back from Paris!' is what both English translations use and 'my master' cannot serve as a vocative.

Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!.finding: Title of Part I, chapter XIII (XV in the fuller 1929/2013 text) of Двенадцать стульев. In the novel the line is not Ostap's and not a doctor's: it is the stock command of a Moscow newsreel director in a leather shirt who, at the Stargorod tram opening, films ordinary citizens as 'passengers' and shouts 'Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!.. Коля! Ноги крупно!' to each of them in turn; the joke is canned emotion ordered up for the camera. Ostap does not say the words in the chapter (his laugh there is at Gavrilin's 'buying a donkey' remark); the attribution to Bender comes from popular memory and the film adaptations. By 2013 it was a fully proverbial ironic phrase used to tell someone to calm down / stop overdramatising, listed in Russian 'крылатые выражения' collections. Established renderings: Richardson (lib.ru) 'Breathe Deeper: You're Excited!'; Fisher (Northwestern 2011) 'Breathe Deeper, You're Excited!'; Shanghai Yiwen zh edition '请深呼吸：您太激动啦！'; Xu Changhan (2022) '深呼吸：您是很激动的！'. No Japanese rendering of the chapter title (Egawa Takashi tr.) was findable online.

rendering.ja: 深呼吸を。あなたは興奮しています！

Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!.note_for_reader: A newsreel director's canned instruction to amateur 'passengers'; in Russian it became a proverbial ironic way of saying 'calm down, you're overdoing it'.
Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!.rationale: Kept the flat imperative-plus-diagnosis shape so the title and every in-text repetition can match verbatim, and followed the established English and Chinese translations rather than coining; gave up the later proverbial 'calm down' connotation, which no target language carries and the note supplies. The Japanese is new (no published title found) and kept deliberately mechanical to sound like a stage direction.

богадельня.finding: Богадельня (from Church Slavonic 'бога дѣля', 'for God's sake') is the pre-revolutionary word for a charitable home for the aged and infirm, usually church- or merchant-endowed; Ozhegov also records a colloquial, disapproving figurative sense, 'an institution full of idle, useless people'. In the novel it is never the official name: the institution is the '2-й дом Старсобеса' (2nd House of the Stargorod Social Security Department) in the former Vorobyaninov mansion, run by the 'shy thief' Alkhen (ch. VIII). The word occurs in two mouths: the old yardman Tikhon in ch. V ('У нас тут государственная богадельня: старухи живут на полном пенсионе') — an old-regime man reaching for the old-regime word for the new Soviet institution, which is the joke — and Ostap in ch. IX ('Это стул из богадельни. Куплен сегодня утром за три рубля'), casually dismissive. Existing translations: Richardson (1971) gives 'a home for old-age women pensioners' and 'the chair from the pensioner's home'; Zhang Peiwen's Chinese has 国家养老院 / 养老院的那把椅子 while the institution is 社会保障处第二院; Japanese coverage of the Egawa Takashi translation uses 社会保険局第二養老院 / 第二養老院. So the established target-language renderings are plain 'old people's home' words; the archaic, faintly ironic tinge of богадельня is generally dropped.
богадельня.note_for_reader: Богадельня is the old church-charity word for a poorhouse for the aged; the yardman uses it for the new Soviet 'Social Security House' in the Vorobyaninov mansion, which is the same old women's home seen in the earlier chapters.
богадельня.rationale: English 'almshouse' keeps the archaic charitable connotation and Tikhon's old-regime register and is still transparent as 'the old women's home' the reader has already met; Chinese 养老院 and Japanese 養老院 follow the established translations and keep denotation and the link to 社会保障处第二院 / 第二養老院, giving up the church-charity tinge (Japanese 養老院 is itself dated, so it keeps some of it), which the one-line note at first occurrence restores.

ГПУ.finding: ГПУ (Государственное политическое управление, State Political Directorate) was the Soviet secret police created on 6 February 1922 as the direct successor of the Cheka, under Dzerzhinsky; on 15 November 1923 it became the all-Union ОГПУ (OGPU), and in July 1934 it was folded into the NKVD. In 1927-28, when the novel is set, the body was formally the OGPU, but everyday speech kept saying 'ГПУ', and the three letters carried the same chill as 'Cheka' had: arrest, search, the knock at the door. In the novel it appears in Ostap's deadpan threat to Vorobyaninov, 'Вам некуда торопиться. ГПУ к вам само придёт', which became a proverb; John Richardson's 1961 English version flattens this to 'The secret police will come for you, anyway', losing the acronym. Reference works fix the target-language forms: English 'GPU'/'State Political Directorate' (Wikipedia), Chinese 国家政治保卫局 with transliteration 格伯乌/格别乌 (zh Wikipedia), Japanese 国家政治保安部 with the dictionary-attested reading ゲーペーウー (Daijisen, ja Wikipedia). Note: the brief's instruction to check coverage of 'Durov and VKontakte around 2013' does not match this 1928 term and was treated as a template slip; the term was researched for 1920s Soviet readers.
ГПУ.note_for_reader: GPU / 格伯乌 / ゲーペーウー: the Soviet secret police of 1922-34 (successor of the Cheka, predecessor of the NKVD); on first occurrence render as 'the GPU (the secret police)' / '格伯乌（国家政治保卫局，即秘密警察）' / 'ゲーペーウー（国家政治保安部、秘密警察）', thereafter the bare short form.
ГПУ.rationale: All three keep the denotation and the acronym's connotation of dread as a short, sayable name, with a one-time gloss so the non-specialist reader is never lost; given up is the formal full title in running text (bland and long) and, in English, the technically correct 1928 form 'OGPU', since the characters say ГПУ and 'GPU' is the established reference-work form.

Маслоцентр.finding: Маслоцентр was the telescoped name of the Всероссийский союз молочной кооперации (All-Russian Union of Dairy Cooperatives), the central body that bought, graded and exported the butter of the peasant dairy artels; it began work on 1 July 1924, won a gold medal for butter quality at the 1926 International Dairy Congress, pushed the cooperative share of butter procurement from about 50% (1924/25) to 75% (1928/29), and was merged away in the December 1929 reorganisation of dairy and livestock cooperation, being liquidated in 1930. In the novel it appears once, in Chapter 5 (Stargorod market): the detective ignores Bender's astrolabe because it looks nothing like the typewriter stolen the day before from Маслоцентр. For a 1928 reader it was a familiar, slightly comic specimen of the Soviet '-центр' acronym-office (Хлебоцентр, Колхозцентр), a real institution from which a typewriter could plausibly go missing; the joke is the deadpan bureaucratic precision, not the butter. Existing renderings: Richardson's 1961 English gives 'the Central Union of Dairy Co-operatives'; Zhang Peiwen's Chinese gives '脂油中心' (odd, since 脂油 suggests lard); no Japanese rendering could be verified online (Egawa Taku's 1969 translation is not indexed), and Fisher's 2011 English could not be checked.
Маслоцентр.note_for_reader: Maslotsentr: the All-Russian Union of Dairy Cooperatives (1924–30), the state-backed butter-marketing body; one of the era's many '-tsentr' acronym offices.
Маслоцентр.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a central butter/dairy organisation) and the mock-official Soviet-acronym register by using a short institutional compound ('Centre' / 总社 / 中央組合) rather than Richardson's long official title; they give up the exact 'cooperative union' structure and the acronym form itself, and the English drops the parenthetical transliteration because the Russian line sits beside it in this edition.

Лед тронулся, господа присяжные заседате.finding: Ostap Bender's signature exclamation, first used in the 'Diamond Smoke' chapter when Vorobyaninov tells him about the jewels (he jumps up and says it to the iron stove) and repeated book-wide, often paired with 'Заседание продолжается!'. 'Лед тронулся' is the ordinary Russian image of the spring ice-break on a river, long used figuratively for 'things have finally started moving / the breakthrough has come' (Chekhov uses it literally in 'На реке'). 'Господа присяжные заседатели' is the formal address of counsel to a jury under the 1864 imperial court reform; juries were abolished by the Soviet Decree on Courts No. 1 (1917/18), so in 1928 the address is a mock-solemn, deliberately obsolete pre-revolutionary flourish aimed at an audience of one (Kisa) or none, which is the joke. Established English coverage (Wikipedia 'Ostap Bender', gw2ru) uses 'The ice has broken, gentlemen of the jury!'; Richardson's 1961 translation flattens it to 'Things are moving, gentlemen of the jury', and Fisher's 2011 version is reported (search snippet, not verified against the book) as 'The ice has started breaking up, gentlemen of the jury!'. I could not verify the wording in a published Chinese or Japanese translation online; Chinese coverage of the new editions quotes the companion catchphrase as '庭审继续进行'.

rendering.en: The ice has broken, gentlemen of the jury!
rendering.zh: 冰河解冻了，陪审员先生们！
rendering.ja: 氷が動き出したぞ、陪審員諸君！

Лед тронулся, господа присяжные заседате.note_for_reader: Ostap addresses his one-man audience with the pre-revolutionary formula for a jury; jury trials had been abolished in 1917, so the courtroom solemnity is a joke he repeats all through the book.
Лед тронулся, господа присяжные заседате.rationale: All three keep the ice-break image (denotation) and the mock-courtroom address (register), fixed verbatim for every occurrence; the perfective 'has broken' / '解冻了' / '動き出した' is chosen over the proposed 'is breaking' so the line reads as Ostap's announcement of a done deal, and the established English wording is preferred over Richardson's 'Things are moving'. Given up: the archaic 1864-era flavour of 'господа присяжные заседатели', which no target language can carry without the note.

Старсобес.finding: Старсобес is a fictional Soviet-style syllabic acronym for Старгородский отдел социального обеспечения, the Stargorod (a made-up provincial town) department of social security; собес itself was a real, colloquially used abbreviation for the local social-welfare office, born of the 1919–1920 reorganisation that created the Narkomat of Social Security and its local отделы собеса. In the novel it appears almost only as '2-й дом Старсобеса' (Old People's Home No. 2 of Starsobes), the former Vorobyaninov mansion run by the 'bashful thief' Alchen (ch. VIII, 'Голубой воришка'); the derivative 'собесовский слесарь' also occurs. For a Russian reader the word is instantly legible as bureaucratic acronym-speak and carries the deadpan irony of a charity office that is really a den of petty theft; 'собес' remained everyday Russian into the 2010s (still used for pension/welfare offices), so the joke needed no explanation. English translators split: Richardson (1961) expands it as 'the Second Home of Stargorod Social Security Administration', Fisher (2011, Northwestern) as 'the Second Stargorod Social Security Home'; neither keeps the acronym. The 1966 Egawa Japanese translation is reported (secondhand) to use '社会保険局第二養老院'. No Chinese rendering of the acronym could be verified online; the Chinese editions were located but not their text.

rendering.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社保局（“斯塔尔索别斯”）
rendering.ja: スタルソベス（スタルゴロド社会保障局）

Старсобес.note_for_reader: Starsobes = STARgorod SOcial SEcurity: a typical Soviet syllabic acronym; 'sobes' remained everyday Russian for the welfare office.
Старсобес.rationale: Expand once with the parenthetical, then keep the short form ('Starsobes Home No. 2' / 社保局第二养老院 / スタルソベス第二養老院) so the acronym-parody and bureaucratic register survive; English and Japanese keep the Soviet acronym sound by transliteration, while Chinese leads with the expansion and borrows the modern abbreviation 社保局 to carry the officialese flavour, giving up the sound of the Russian acronym after first mention.

Знойная женщина — мечта поэта.finding: It is the title of Part I, chapter 12 of Ilf and Petrov's Двенадцать стульев (1927/28) and Ostap Bender's line about the widow Gritsatsuyeva: «Знойная женщина, — сказал Остап, — мечта поэта. Провинциальная непосредственность». Russian dictionaries of winged words (Serov; Большой словарь русских поговорок) list it as a proverbial, jocular-ironic label for an ardent, temperamental, showy woman, and by 2013 it was a fully lexicalised catchphrase used without any thought of the novel. The joke is that Ostap dresses a plump, credulous provincial widow he means to rob in the clichéd lyricism of pre-revolutionary magazine verse. Existing English translations both use 'passionate': Richardson (1961) 'A Passionate Woman Is a Poet's Dream'; Fisher (2011, Northwestern) 'A Passionate Woman, a Poet's Dream' (the latter reported in search summaries, not verified against the printed book). The current Chinese translation (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022) titles the chapter 热情似火的女人是诗人的梦想. No Japanese rendering of the line could be found online; Egawa Takashi's 十二の椅子 (筑摩書房 1969/1977) exists but its chapter titles are not indexed.

rendering.en: A Passionate Woman, a Poet's Dream
rendering.zh: 热情似火的女人是诗人的梦想

Знойная женщина — мечта поэта.note_for_reader: Ostap's mock-lyrical label for the widow became a Russian proverb for a plump, ardent provincial woman.
Знойная женщина — мечта поэта.rationale: Preserved the established English and Chinese renderings (both keyed on 'passionate', usable unchanged as heading and as Ostap's spoken line) and the mock-poetic register; gave up the 'sultry/heat' image of знойная and, for Japanese, the backing of a verified published rendering.

«Титаник».finding: In Chapter VII (numbered IX in the full 1928 text), «Титаник» is the brand name of the contraband hair dye Vorobyaninov buys from a chemist for 3 r. 12 k.: it promises a 'radical black' that 'does not wash out with cold or hot water, soap or kerosene', but comes out with a green tinge; Bender says 'all contraband is made in Odessa, on Malaya Arnautskaya Street' and that 'your «Титаник» is good for nothing, only for dyeing dogs'. Mixed with his own «Наяда», it turns Kisa's head and moustache 'the colours of the solar spectrum', so the chapter title «Следы «Титаника»» (Traces of the «Titanic») puns on the wreck of 1912 — a grand name, a catastrophe, and its lingering traces. Russian readers today (and in 2013, after Cameron's film) read the pun instantly; the joke is the mismatch between the imposing name and the shoddy Odessa fake. The word is always in quotation marks in the Russian, as a brand. Existing renderings are settled: English translations (Richardson on lib.ru; Fisher's 2011 edition) use 'Titanic' / 'the Titanic', chapter 'Traces of the Titanic'; the Chinese edition uses “泰坦尼克”, the standard Mainland transliteration of the ship; no online text of Egawa Taku's Japanese 十二の椅子 was found, but 「タイタニック」 is the only Japanese name of the ship. (The task text's mention of '2013', 'Durov' and 'VKontakte' does not apply to this 1928 novel and was ignored.)
«Титаник».note_for_reader: «Титаник» is the brand of a contraband hair dye; the name evokes the ship that sank in 1912, and the chapter title plays on that.
«Титаник».rationale: The ship's name transliterates identically in all three languages, so denotation (a brand), connotation (grand name, disaster) and the mock-solemn register all survive; quotation marks are kept everywhere to mark it as a brand and to keep 'victim of the «Titanic»' and 'Traces of the «Titanic»' recognisably the same word. Nothing is given up except the mild surprise a 1928 reader felt at a fresh, not yet clichéd, Titanic joke.

Старгород.finding: Старгород is the fictional provincial town where Part One ('Старгородский лев' / 'The Lion of Stargorod') is set: Vorobyaninov's home town, entered by Bender from the village of Chmarovka, site of the 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare' and the May Day tram opening. The name is transparently Old-Russian/Church-Slavonic 'Old Town' (стар- + город), which signals a sleepy pre-revolutionary district seat; it is also a literary borrowing, since Leskov's 'Соборяне' (1872) is set in a provincial Старгород, so for a well-read Russian it carried a faintly archaic, patriarchal, 'old Russia' flavour that the Soviet bustle of the 1920s is being laid over. Local tradition and Russian Wikipedia treat Starobelsk (Luhansk region) as the prototype, but the town is invented and readers do not identify it with a real map point. Existing translations transliterate: John Richardson's English (1961) and later English coverage use 'Stargorod'; Egawa Takashi's Japanese (Shueisha, 1966) uses スタルゴロド; Chinese coverage transliterates 斯塔尔戈罗德, although Xu Changhan's 2021 Chinese edition renders the Part One title as '老城名流' (Old Town Notables), i.e. translates the name at least there.
Старгород.note_for_reader: Stargorod, literally 'Old Town', is an invented provincial town (Leskov had used the same name); its likely model is Starobelsk in eastern Ukraine.
Старгород.rationale: Transliteration in all three languages keeps the denotation (a proper name, consistent across the whole novel and distinct from any real place) and matches the established English and Japanese renderings and the dominant Chinese one; it gives up the transparent 'Old Town' connotation and the Leskov echo, which are recovered once by the one-line note rather than by a translated name that would read as a generic common noun in every sentence.

Востриковы.finding: Plural of the surname of Father Fyodor Vostrikov (отец Фёдор Востриков), priest of the church of Frol and Lavr, the third treasure-hunter; in chapter III it denotes the household of the priest and his wife (попадья Катерина Александровна): 'Сундучок Востриковых, к неудовольствию отца Федора, также был оклеен картинками...' — the couple's little trunk, papered inside by the priest's wife with cuttings from 'Летопись войны 1914 года', an ironic contrast to the Red Army soldier's trunk with Budyonny and the Batum beauties. The surname is an ordinary Russian one (from вострый, 'sharp'), carrying a faint comic hint of sharp-witted, restless scheming that suits the candle-factory dreamer; no reader needs it explained. Richardson's English (1961) has 'The Vostrikovs' trunk'; Fisher (2011) also uses Vostrikov. A Chinese edition (seen only in a search snippet, page not openable) gives the priest as 费奥多尔·沃斯特利科夫; a Japanese reviewer of Egawa Taku's translation writes フョードル・ボストリコフ神父, the older ボ convention for В. Both target languages transliterate; none translates the meaning.
Востриковы.rationale: Denotation (the priest's household, i.e. the couple) and neutral register are kept by a plural family name in English and by surname + 夫妇/夫妻 in Chinese and Japanese, spelled exactly as Vostrikov/沃斯特里科夫/ヴォストリコフ elsewhere in the edition (modern ヴ rather than Egawa-era ボ; standard 新华社 里 rather than the variant 利); the faint 'sharp' etymology of the name is given up, as every existing translation gives it up.

Паша Эмильевич.finding: Fictional character in chapter VIII of «Двенадцать стульев»: a thirty-two-year-old 'двоюродный племянник' of Alkhen's wife Sashkhen who lives as a lodger in the 2nd Stargorod almshouse (Дом собеса) alongside Alkhen's four brothers, wears the same mouse-grey cloth as the old women, steals whatever Alkhen has not stolen himself, once ate two kilograms (1928 text: five pounds) of тюлька at one sitting, and sells the almshouse's chairs out the back door to a dealer — which is how one of the twelve chairs leaves the house. The name is a running joke: 'Паша' is the nursery diminutive of Павел, and welding it to a full patronymic ('Эмильевич', from the un-Russian, faintly foreign 'Эмиль') gives a grown parasite the naming of a spoilt child treated as a respectable adult; the old women garble it further. Commentators (cited on Russian Wikipedia) trace the combination to Dostoevsky's household: his gluttonous stepson Pasha Isaev, who lived with Emilia Fyodorovna Dostoevskaya. By 2013 'Паша Эмильевич, обладавший сверхъестественным чутьём' and 'Кто-нибудь брал у тебя стул?' were stock quotations for a brazen freeloader caught red-handed. John Richardson's standard English translation (1961/1971, text on lib.ru) renders him 'Pasha Emilevich' throughout (once, in an old woman's mouth, 'Pasha Melentevich'). I could not access the text of any Chinese translation (费明君 1954, 安郁琛/钟鼎 1984, 徐昌翰, 张佩文, 白桦熊 2022) or of 江川卓's Japanese translation (集英社 1966), so the zh/ja forms below follow standard transliteration practice rather than a verified published precedent.

rendering.ja: パーシャ・エミーリエヴィチ

Паша Эмильевич.note_for_reader: 'Pasha' is a child's pet-form of Pavel; pairing it with a formal patronymic, for a 32-year-old freeloader, is the authors' joke — like calling a grown man 'Little Paulie, Esq.'
Паша Эмильевич.rationale: Keeps denotation (a fixed proper name, in the established Richardson spelling for English and standard 新华社/カタカナ transliteration for zh and ja) and the full diminutive-plus-patronymic form so the incongruity survives on the page; gives up the automatic comic register, since none of the three languages hears 'Pasha' as babyish or 'Emilevich' as pompous, and restores it with a one-line note rather than by domesticating the name.

Голубой воришка.finding: Title of the chapter (VIII in the 1928 book text, IX in the full-manuscript edition) introducing Alkhen, manager of the Second Stargorod Social Security Home, who steals from his old women constantly and blushes constantly: 'застенчивый воришка... Крал он постоянно, постоянно стыдился'. In 1920s literary Russian 'голубой' applied to a person meant naive, tender, pure-hearted, romantically innocent (a colour of German-Romantic idealism), and the joke is the oxymoron of an innocent-souled embezzler; there is no sexual sense, which голубой acquired only later in Soviet slang. The phrase became a proverb, used 'шутливо, иронически о робком воре с приятной внешностью и обходительными манерами' (citaty.su). Existing renderings: John Richardson (1961) 'The Bashful Chiseller'; Anne O. Fisher (2011) 'The Little Sky-Blue Thief' (literal, keeps the colour but is opaque to English readers); Chinese Zhang Peiwen (人民文学) '文过饰非的小偷' and a newer edition '知耻无悔的小偷', both of which shift the sense toward glossing over or shamelessness rather than bashfulness; no Japanese chapter title (江川卓訳『十二の椅子』) could be located online. The brief's mention of Durov/VKontakte and 2013 is a template error and irrelevant to this term.
Голубой воришка.note_for_reader: Голубой ('sky-blue') in 1920s Russian meant innocent, pure-hearted; the title is an oxymoron, an innocent-souled embezzler, and the phrase became a Russian byword for a thief with meek manners.
Голубой воришка.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a petty thief, diminutive воришка) and the ironic, mock-tender connotation of bashfulness that the chapter turns on, following Richardson's sense rather than Fisher's literal colour; the colour word itself and its 1920s Romantic tint are given up, since 'blue/蓝/青' would mislead or mean nothing, and the note carries that residue. The Chinese departs from both published titles because they invert the meaning.

архивариус.finding: Архивариус (Latin archivarius) is the pre-revolutionary Russian title for the official in charge of an archive; it entered Russian law under Peter I's General Regulation for the Colleges (1720) and by the 1766 Senate rule such men were to be 'of sober conduct, above suspicion'. In the novel it is how Varfolomei Korobeinikov, 'a former official of the city governor's chancery, now a clerical worker', introduces himself: 'Я — архивариус в Старкомхозе' (ch. XI, 'Alphabet — Mirror of Life'); he privately hoards the requisition orders for nationalised furniture and sells them to Bender and to Father Fyodor. By 1928 the word was already an old-regime civil-service term: Ushakov (1935) still glosses it 'заведующий архивом', but the 20th century replaced it with the plain 'архивист', so the Latinate ending gives the little pawnbroker-bureaucrat a mock-solemn, Gogolian dignity (critics compare the scene to Chichikov and Sobakevich). English coverage of the character uniformly calls him 'the archivist' / 'Archivist Korobeinikov'. I could not reach the text of the Chinese (张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2022) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) translations to confirm their exact wording, so the zh and ja choices rest on dictionary usage rather than an attested published rendering.
архивариус.rationale: All three keep the denotation (keeper of an institutional archive) and the formal, official-title register, which is what lets the mock-solemn joke of a tiny hoarder calling himself by a Petrine civil-service title survive; the specifically dated, old-regime colour of the Latin -arius ending is given up in every language, since 'archivist', 档案管理员 and 文書保管係 are all current words, and a note would kill the joke. For zh I keep the proposed 档案管理员 (standard dictionary equivalent, immediately clear); for ja I prefer 文書保管係 over the proposed 文書係, which reads as a generic paperwork clerk and loses the 'keeper of records' sense the plot turns on.

«Быстроупак».finding: «Быстроупак» is the small private firm of the ex-merchant Dyadyev in Stargorod (ch. XIV, 'Союз меча и орала'): he is introduced as «хозяин „Быстроупака“ Дядьев», paired with Kislarsky, chairman of the «Одесская бубличная артель „Московские баранки“»; the narrators add that both were really cloth traders. The name is a fictional telescoped compound, быстро + упак(овка) 'quick-pack(ing)', built exactly like the state acronym-agencies of the 1920s (Главупак, Мосторг), so the joke for a Russian reader was a NEPman aping Soviet institutional nomenclature while doing ordinary trade; it recurs when the 'fine young men from Quickpack' queue at the flour shop. In English it has two established calques: John Richardson (1961) 'Fastpack' and Anne O. Fisher (2011) 'Quickpack'; both translate rather than transliterate. No established Chinese or Japanese rendering was found in web coverage of the novel.
«Быстроупак».note_for_reader: A made-up firm name telescoped from 'quick' + 'packing', mocking the acronym style of Soviet agencies of the 1920s.
«Быстроупак».rationale: Calque in all three languages, following Fisher's established 'Quickpack' rather than a transliteration, because the humour lives in the recognisable telescoping and the side-by-side Russian already supplies the sound; the Soviet-acronym flavour is carried by the compact one-word form (公司/社 mark it as a firm) and the note, while the specific NEP-era resonance of a private firm wearing a state-style name is given up.

Перелешинский переулок.finding: A fictional side street in the fictional provincial town of Stargorod; no real street of that name is documented in Odessa, Moscow or the towns proposed as Stargorod's prototype (Starobelsk, Voronezh, Noginsk). In the Russian text (ch. X) house No. 7 on the lane is a shabby two-storey Second-Empire building with eight chipped lion heads 'strikingly resembling the writer Artsybashev'; both the locksmith Viktor Polesov (workshop in the second courtyard) and the fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna Bour live there, and in ch. XIII Polesov leads the concessionaires back to it by way of connecting yards, Ostap perching on a gate of No. 5. The name is built on the gentry surname Perelyoshin/Pereleshin (a Voronezh and Kostroma noble family), so for a 1928 reader it sounded like a typical pre-revolutionary provincial street named after a local landowner, faintly genteel and faded, which fits its role as the nest of the 'Sword and Ploughshare' monarchist conspiracy. English precedent is split: the older Richardson-derived online text uses 'Pereleshinsky Street', Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation uses 'Pereleshinsky Lane'. No established Chinese or Japanese rendering was found in searchable coverage of the 张佩文 (2004) or 江川卓 (1969) translations.
Перелешинский переулок.rationale: Denotation (a small side street, distinct from улица/street) is kept in all three by binding переулок to Lane / 巷 / 横丁 book-wide, with the adjectival -ский reduced to the stem in zh and ja as is normal for Russian street names in those languages; the faint 'named-after-a-landowner' connotation is given up, since no target reader would catch it and a note would cost more than it pays.

Ипполит Матвеевич.finding: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov is the co-protagonist of The Twelve Chairs: a 52-year-old former uyezd (district) marshal of the nobility (уездный предводитель дворянства, from 1912), reduced after 1917 to running the deaths-and-marriages desk at the ZAGS registry in the town of N, who hunts his mother-in-law's jewels with Ostap Bender; Bender calls him by his childhood nickname Kisa. The narrator's fixed form is the full name plus patronymic, a mock-respectful, faintly old-regime formality that Russian readers hear as part of the joke; the name Ippolit itself is an aristocratic, pre-revolutionary choice. Commentators note a resemblance to the Kadet politician Pavel Milyukov (and readers guessed Bunin), and the name is a running proverb in Russian culture. Established renderings: English editions and Wikipedia use Ippolit Matveyevich (Fisher 2011 and Richardson 1961 both keep the patronymic); the Chinese translation by 张佩文 (人民文学出版社, 2004; Shanghai Translation 2022 by 白桦熊 also exists) uses 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 and 沃洛比亚尼诺夫; Japanese coverage is thin, the 1969 江川卓 translation is out of print and a fan review spells him イポリット・マトベイッチ, so there is no single fixed katakana form and a standard transliteration must be chosen.

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

Ипполит Матвеевич.note_for_reader: Russian narrators address adults by first name plus patronymic (father's name + -ovich/-evich); the novel never shortens him, and the formality is part of the joke.
Ипполит Матвеевич.rationale: All three keep the denotation and the narrator's mock-formal name-plus-patronymic register by transliterating in full (no surname substitution, no ja honorific such as さん); what is lost is the instant Russian sense of the patronymic as a courtesy form, which the one-line note supplies, and in ja the lack of a canonical spelling means we bind a standard transliteration rather than an inherited one.

Коробейников.finding: Варфоломей Коробейников is the archivist of Part One, ch. XI ('Алфавит — Зеркало жизни'): 'бывший чиновник канцелярии градоначальства, ныне работник конторского труда', who once served in the Старкомхоз archive and quietly took home the ордера (allocation warrants) for furniture requisitioned after 1917, keeping them in an alphabetised cabinet and selling the information to former owners.
