Bender concludes 'старик — типичная сволочь'; commentators (Odessky/Feldman, Shcheglov) read the scene as a parody of Chichikov haggling with Sobakevich over dead souls, since the furniture exists only on paper, and a cut manuscript passage had him insuring his grandmother's life for profit. The surname is an ordinary Russian one from коробейник 'pedlar', a faint joke (a man peddling paper goods) that no Russian reader treats as a speaking name. The Richardson English translation (Sphere 1971, Northwestern reprint) uses 'Korobeinikov' and 'The Mirror-of-Life Index' for the chapter; a few English fan pages write 'Korobeynikov'. I could not access the text of the Chinese (张佩文 2004; 徐昌翰 2022) or Japanese (江川卓 1966/1969) translations to verify their spelling of this minor name, so the zh/ja forms below are the standard transliterations, not confirmed published ones.
Коробейников.rationale: Denotation and register are kept by a plain, consistent transliteration matching Richardson's established English form; the faint 'pedlar' etymology is given up in all three languages, as a Russian reader barely registers it and the archivist's trade in paper furniture carries the joke on its own.

Гусище.finding: Гусище is a fictional outlying district (окраина) of the fictional town of Stargorod in Ilf and Petrov's novel, not a real place. Chapter XI introduces it as where the archivist Korobeinikov lives: 'Коробейников жил на Гусище — окраине Старгорода. Там жили преимущественно железнодорожники', with a snorting locomotive backing along an embankment fenced with thin concrete panels and a railway workers' club nearby. In Chapter XIII it is the site of the tramway depot: in 1920 depot workers and rope-makers went there 'с музыкой' for subbotniki and dug holes all day, and on May Day the concessionaires walk with the demonstrations 'до Гусища' for the tram opening. For a Russian reader the name sounds like a rustic village-toponym (root гусь 'goose' plus the place/augmentative suffix -ище, cf. Городище, Головище), signalling a shabby working-class railway edge of town rather than any literal goose meaning; a Nizhny Novgorod forum thread compares it to the real village Gusevo, but that page could not be opened and the identification is speculative. No published English, Chinese or Japanese rendering of this specific name was found online; Anne O. Fisher's 2011 English translation exists but its wording for this name was not verifiable via search, so the standard transliteration is the defensible choice.
Гусище.note_for_reader: Gusishche: a fictional railway-workers' district on the edge of Stargorod; the name has a village-like ring (from 'goose' + a place suffix).
Гусище.rationale: Kept denotation and register by treating it as a proper name transliterated by the standard systems (BGN/PCGR-style Latin, 俄汉译音表 for Chinese, conventional katakana with シチェ for -ще), consistent with Stargorod and other toponyms in earlier chapters; gave up the faint rustic 'goose' connotation, which no target-language coinage could carry without sounding like a joke the original does not make.

Полесов.finding: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov is a fictional Stargorod character introduced in chapter X ('Слесарь, попугай и гадалка'): a self-employed 'artisan with a motor' (кустарь-одиночка с мотором) who runs a mechanical workshop full of dead forges and broken parts, takes on jobs he never finishes (the gates of house No. 5), lectures everyone on tram-building and 3/8-inch dies, and is the first recruit and loudest member of Bender's sham 'Sword and Ploughshare' conspiracy. The narrators fix him with two oxymoronic epithets that became proverbial in Russian: слесарь-интеллигент (со средним образованием) and кипучий лентяй, 'the seething idler'; хлопотливый ('fussy, bustling') recurs as his tag. For a Russian reader by 2013 'Полесов' is a byword for the know-it-all busybody with opinions on everything and no finished work of his own; livelib and the fan wiki gloss him as 'профессиональный недотёпа'. Richardson's English (1961/1971, lib.ru text) renders him 'Polesov' and the epithet as 'mechanic-intellectual'; Fisher (2011) also keeps 'Polesov'. Search did not surface the exact katakana or hanzi used in Egawa Taku's Japanese translation (1966/1969) or Zhang Peiwen's Chinese (人民文学出版社, 2004), so the zh/ja forms below follow standard transliteration practice rather than a verified printed page.
Полесов.note_for_reader: Polesov, the 'mechanic-intellectual' and 'seething idler' of Stargorod: a Soviet byword for the busybody handyman who has opinions on everything and finishes nothing.
Полесов.rationale: The surname is a plain proper name, so all three languages keep denotation by transliteration (matching Richardson/Fisher in English and the standard zh/ja conventions for -ов names); the connotation lives in the epithets, which must be bound once and kept stable: en 'mechanic-intellectual' / 'seething idler' / 'the fussy mechanic', zh '钳工知识分子' / '忙忙碌碌的钳工', ja 'インテリ錠前屋' / 'せわしない錠前屋'. The proverbial weight of the name for Russians is given up and carried by the one-line note.

Треухов.finding: Треухов is the fictional Stargorod engineer of Chapter XIII ("Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!"): he conceived the city tramway in 1912, was refused by the Tsarist duma, then by the war and revolution, then by the new communal-services chief Gavrilin ("in Samarkand we don't need trams"), and finally builds it while being pilloried by a hack journalist. He is the book's one honest, competent worker, and the authors mark him by shyness (he asks the newsreel crew "застенчиво", turns crimson, stammers a speech about the international situation and forgets to mention the tram) and by a sudden drunken tirade at the banquet against the press ("акробаты фарса, гиены пера, виртуозы ротационных машин"), which itself parodies a French Communist's speech he once heard. The surname is a plain Russian one from треух, the old three-flap fur hat, ancestor of the ushanka; it carries a faintly homely, unglamorous sound to a Russian ear but no joke that a reader would need explained, and no real person stands behind it. John Richardson's standard English translation (1961, on lib.ru) spells him Treukhov throughout. I could not open the Chinese (徐昌翰, 江苏凤凰文艺 2022; 上海译文 edition) or Japanese (江川卓, 集英社 1966/1969) translations online, so their in-text spellings are unverified; the proposed 特列乌霍夫 and トレウーホフ follow the standard 新华社 and stress-marking katakana conventions for -ухов names.
Треухов.rationale: Kept denotation and the neutral register of an ordinary surname by transliterating consistently in all three languages, matching Richardson's established English form; gave up the faint fur-hat etymology, which no Russian reader treats as a pun and which no rendering could carry without a heavier joke than the original makes. The character's unity across pages rests on translating застенчиво/заалелся and the drunken speech consistently, not on the name.

Елена Станиславовна.finding: Elena Stanislavovna Bour (Боур) is a minor character of The Twelve Chairs: the wife of a pre-revolutionary prosecutor and Vorobyaninov's old flame (the affair and a trip to Paris date to 1899-1900), now an ageing, slightly grubby fortune-teller in Stargorod who reads cards and palms for fifty kopecks, keeps a white parrot 'in red underpants', and hosts in her flat the meeting at which Ostap founds the bogus 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare' (chapters X and XIV). The name is a plain name-plus-patronymic, the polite form of address of a formerly genteel lady; the comedy lies in the gap between her faded 'society' pretensions and her present squalor, not in the name itself. Both standard English translations (Richardson 1961; Anne O. Fisher, Northwestern 2011) print 'Elena Stanislavovna'; IMDb lists the 1971 Gaidai film role as 'Yelena Stanislavovna Bour'. I could not verify online how the published Chinese (张佩文 2004; 白桦熊 2022) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) translations spell her name; the proposed zh and ja forms follow the standard 新华社 and katakana transliteration conventions.

rendering.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
rendering.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

Елена Станиславовна.note_for_reader: Name + patronymic (father's name, here 'daughter of Stanislav') is the polite Russian form of address; Elena Stanislavovna is the fortune-teller Madame Bour, Vorobyaninov's pre-revolutionary flame.
Елена Станиславовна.rationale: Keeps denotation and the neutral, polite name-patronymic register by straight transliteration matched to the established English form; the connotation that a patronymic signals respectful address is carried by the one-line note rather than by an English 'Madame', and the surname Bour is left for the sentences where the Russian uses it.

Союз меча и орала.finding: Title of Chapter XIV of Part I and the name of the sham underground monarchist society Ostap Bender improvises in Stargorod to extract 'donations' from Vorobyaninov's frightened former-elite acquaintances, presenting Vorobyaninov as a 'giant of thought, father of Russian democracy'. The name is a pompous White-Guard-sounding pastiche built on Isaiah 2:4 as it is worded in the Russian Synodal Bible ('перековать мечи на орала', beat swords into ploughshares): орало is the archaic Church Slavonic word for a plough, not the verb орать ('to yell'), though the modern comic reading is part of the joke. Russian dictionaries of winged words (Serov; Academic.ru) record it as a fully proverbial phrase used ironically of political organisations that exist only on paper or in their founders' imagination, and of any 'association' set up to relieve the gullible of money. Established renderings: John Richardson's English translation (the widely circulated one) titles the chapter 'The Alliance of the Sword and Ploughshare' and English Wikipedia uses the same; the standard Chinese translation by 张佩文 (人民文学出版社) titles Chapter 14 '剑犁同盟', which is the form used by Chinese readers on Douban. No online text of 江川卓's Japanese translation (筑摩書房, 1969) was found, so no established Japanese chapter title could be verified; the 新共同訳 Bible renders Isaiah 2:4 as '剣を打ち直して鋤とし', making 鋤 the recognisable biblical word.

rendering.en: The Alliance of the Sword and Ploughshare

Союз меча и орала.note_for_reader: A mock-solemn name built on Isaiah's 'swords into ploughshares' (орало is an archaic word for plough); in Russian the phrase became a byword for a paper organisation founded to fleece its members.
Союз меча и орала.rationale: Kept the biblical denotation (sword + ploughshare in each language's Bible wording) and the pompous, faintly White-Guard register of a 'Union/Alliance', and bound the established chapter titles of the Richardson and 张佩文 translations rather than coining new ones; gave up the untranslatable Russian pun on орать 'to yell' and the proverbial status the phrase has for Russians, which the note supplies.

conventions: Soviet address 'гражданин/гражданка' is always 'Citizen' (公民 / 市民), never Mr/Mrs; 'господин/госпожа/мадам' keep their genteel or ironic flavour as Mr/Mrs/Madame. [rank 46]
Russian dialogue dashes become English quotation marks, zh 「」or “”, ja 「」; narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the same sentence, not footnoted. [rank 46]
Bender's recurring catchphrases (гражданин, господа присяжные заседатели, концессия, сын турецкого подданного) are bound once and repeated verbatim in all three languages. [rank 46]
Dialogue: keep the Russian em-dash dialogue lines in English; use 「」 in Japanese and “” in Chinese, one exchange per paragraph as in the original. [rank 15]

ты/вы: Bender's instant ты to Tikhon and Tikhon's reply in ты are rendered in Japanese with plain (だ/である) forms and 'おまえ/あんた'; in English mark familiarity with 'grandad' and contractions rather than pronouns. [rank 15]
Soviet acronyms (АХРР, Стардеткомиссия etc.): transliterate the acronym and give the expansion in brackets at first occurrence per chapter; thereafter acronym alone. [rank 15]
Dialogue: Russian em-dash speech becomes double quotation marks in en, “ ” in zh, 「 」 in ja; the narrator's interjections inside a speech stay inline, not as separate lines. [rank 30]

Vorobyaninov and Father Fyodor keep formal вы even while brawling and spitting; render with full 'Father'/'Ippolit Matveyevich' address in en, 您 in zh, and です/ます plus 神父 in ja, so the comic politeness survives. [rank 30]

Bender's corporate parody vocabulary (концессия, концессионер, технический директор, компаньон) is a fixed set rendered with business terms and never explained or varied; Russian names are transliterated consistently without added Japanese honorifics. [rank 30]

Ostap's recruiting formulas (Крепитесь; В каком полку служили?; Заграница/Запад нам поможет; Полная тайна организации) are rendered with one fixed wording per language everywhere in the book, since the comedy is repetition [rank 60]

Dialogue dashes become English double quotes, Chinese “ ”, Japanese 「 」; the narrator's asides and characters' inner speech in «» stay as quotation marks (en single, zh “ ”, ja 「 」) rather than italics [rank 60]

Japanese: narrator in plain form (だ・である), Ostap addresses recruits in polite です・ます with mock-solemn ください; Russian names kept in katakana with long vowels marked and name-and-patronymic preserved where the Russian uses it [rank 60]

Pre-revolutionary ranks and titles (граф, княгиня, гусар) are rendered with their standard aristocratic equivalents (Count/伯爵/伯爵, Princess/公爵夫人/公爵夫人) and never modernised or dropped; the city stays 'Petersburg' in the tale of the hussar-monk. [rank 47]

Orthodox church vocabulary (схима, вериги, клобук, пустынь, игумен) is rendered with the plain meaning in the sentence and the Russian term given once in parentheses at first occurrence; no footnotes for these. [rank 47]
